definition: Language crafted to persuade or impress, sometimes with more style than substance.
example: Behind the advertisement's lofty rhetoric about freedom was simply a pricier phone plan.
nuance: Eloquence is almost always praise, but rhetoric often hints that the fine words may be hollow or insincere.
prompt: A student is preparing her closing speech for a debate tournament.
options: Her coach taught her the rhetoric of a strong close: restate the claim and end on a vivid image.
When the judge asked a rhetoric, the debater paused, knowing no answer was expected.
Her rhetoric consisted of reading the timer aloud every thirty seconds and nothing else during the round.
Before the final round, she rhetoric her opponent's weakest points until the audience agreed with her.
reasons: Techniques for shaping words so they persuade an audience are exactly what this noun names.
This confuses the noun with a rhetorical question; the word does not name a single question.
Announcing the time is not persuasive or impressive language of any kind.
The word is a noun, so it cannot serve as the verb of a sentence.

practice.prompt: A critic reviews a grand speech given at a school's anniversary gala.
options: The critic praised the speaker's soaring rhetoric but noted that the speech announced no actual plans.
The speaker's rhetoric was a silent slideshow of tuition figures, shown without a single spoken or written word.
The critic said the gala's rhetoric was far too salty and needed a squeeze of lemon before serving.
The critic found the anniversary speech very rhetoric, with flourishes stacked on top of flourishes.
reasons: Impressive language that lacks concrete substance fits the word and its frequent hint of hollowness.
Persuasive language needs words; a wordless display of numbers is the opposite.
Treating the word as a dish to be seasoned ignores that it refers to language.
The adjective form is rhetorical; the noun cannot describe a speech after very.
